Rationale (correct, baseline-focused): In RB1-proficient tumors, CDK4/6-mediated RB phosphorylation releases E2F, inducing DNA replication genes (polymerases, MCMs, CDC6, etc.). Abemaciclib blocks RB phosphorylation, re-pressing E2F targets. Moderate to high E2F-target expression reflecting active but RB-dependent cycling tends to mark tumors that respond; extreme E2F activation via RB loss/c-MYC can bypass CDK4/6 and confer resistance.

ER signaling induces CCND1 (cyclin D1) and promotes CDK4/6 activity. Luminal ER⁺/HER2– tumors with intact ER signaling and dependence on estrogen-driven cyclin D1 show the greatest benefit from ET + CDK4/6i; ET plus abemaciclib suppresses ER target genes and cell cycle. Loss of ER or an “ER-low/non-luminal” phenotype associates with poorer CDK4/6i benefit.

Overexpression/amplification of cyclin D1 (CCND1) or high CDK4/6 levels mark tumors that rely on this axis for RB phosphorylation and G1–S entry. Such tumors are particularly vulnerable to abemaciclib; pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibition reduces pRb and arrests cells in G1.

Cyclin E–CDK2 can maintain RB phosphorylation and drive S-phase entry even when CDK4/6 is inhibited. Clinical and translational data show high CCNE1 expression associates with short PFS and resistance to palbociclib/abemaciclib; low CCNE1 correlates with better outcomes.

RB1 is the canonical target of CDK4/6i. Tumors with RB1 loss-of-function (genomic loss, truncating mutation, complete protein loss) fail to undergo G1 arrest with CDK4/6 blockade and are essentially insensitive to abemaciclib. RB1 loss is a well-described mechanism of both de novo and acquired CDK4/6i resistance.

Activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR supports cell growth and survival independent of cyclin D–CDK4/6, and is enriched in endocrine-resistant tumors. Functional proteomic and resistance-model studies show PI3K/AKT/mTOR upregulation in CDK4/6i-resistant breast cancer; dual CDK4/6 + PI3K/mTOR targeting can restore apoptosis and overcome resistance.

FGFR1 amplification and MAPK activation induce cyclins and CDK6, providing an alternative proliferative drive that bypasses CDK4/6 blockade. In ER⁺ breast cancer, FGFR1-altered models and patients show resistance to ET + CDK4/6i, which can be mitigated by FGFR inhibitors.

CDKN2A/p16^INK4A^ normally inhibits cyclin D–CDK4/6. In many HR⁺ breast cancers, loss of p16 is part of the oncogenic program and may mark CDK4/6 dependence and sensitivity; conversely, high p16 frequently accompanies RB1 dysfunction or other cell-cycle rewiring, correlating with poor response to CDK4/6i in several datasets and xenograft models. Thus “p16 up” is generally a red flag for resistance when it reflects an abnormal RB loop.

CDK4/6 inhibition (including abemaciclib) modulates the tumor immune microenvironment, increasing antigen presentation and T-cell infiltration but also inducing PD-L1 upregulation as a negative feedback. This PD-L1 increase is treatment-associated, not a classic baseline selection marker; it may limit long-term responses unless combined with immune checkpoint blockade. Upregulation is primarily post-treatment/adaptive (CDK4/6i-induced PD-L1 on tumor and immune cells)

Loss of FAT1 impairs Hippo tumor-suppressor signaling, leading to nuclear YAP/TAZ accumulation and transcriptional upregulation of CDK6 and other proliferative genes. Functional genomics screens and clinical correlates in ER⁺ breast cancer show FAT1 and other Hippo alterations as recurrent drivers of CDK4/6i resistance.

TK1 activity reflects S-phase flux and is downstream of CDK4/6–RB–E2F signaling. Patients starting CDK4/6i + ET with high baseline TK1 but showing a robust early decline in TK1 activity have better PFS; persistent or rising TK1 on therapy marks early progression. Thus TK1 is best viewed as a pharmacodynamic marker, with baseline high proliferation compatible with sensitivity but on-treatment decrease being the key favorable sign.
Alpelisib is active when the PI3Kα pathway is activated (PIK3CA driver mutations). Clinical benefit shown in PIK3CA-mutant, HR+ HER2− breast cancer (SOLAR-1). (PubMed)

Elevated mTORC1 output (p-4EBP1/p-S6) can maintain translation/growth and is a documented resistance mechanism to PI3K inhibition; targeting mTORC1 (or using mTORC1-selective inhibitors) can overcome resistance. (PubMed Central)
HER2 activation can drive PI3K signaling and promote therapeutic escape; PI3Kα inhibitors may need combination (HER2 blockade) in HER2+ / PIK3CA settings — monotherapy is often insufficient. (PubMed)

Alpelisib was developed and approved for HR-positive (ER+) PIK3CA-mutant advanced BC in combination with endocrine therapy (fulvestrant); the key predictor is PIK3CA mutation in the HR+ context. The statement “ER signaling Down → Sensitive” confuses treatment effect (ER target down after fulvestrant) with the baseline predictor. (PubMed)

PI3K pathway and downstream AKT/mTOR regulate glucose metabolism; PI3K inhibitor resistance is often accompanied by metabolic rewiring (increased glycolysis or alternate fuel use), and targeting metabolism can sensitize resistant cells in preclinical models. (PubMed Central)

MAPK pathway activation (mutations or RTK feedback) is a well described bypass mechanism to PI3K inhibition; combined PI3K + MAPK axis targeting is a rational strategy in preclinical/clinical work. (PubMed Central)

Relief of AKT survival signaling (BCL2 family, MCL1 modulation) leads to apoptosis in sensitive tumors; however degree of apoptosis varies with tumor context and co-alterations (e.g., PTEN loss, concurrent MAPK activation). (PubMed Central)

Partially Sensitive (context-dependent)  (ESR1 mutations often cause endocrine resistance; alpelisib + fulvestrant can still have activity) ESR1 activating mutations drive endocrine resistance but combining PI3Kα inhibition with ER downregulation (fulvestrant) can have activity in some settings; evidence is mixed and depends on prior therapies (CDK4/6 exposure etc.). ESR1 mutation is not a simple “positive” predictor but combination therapy may work in some ESR1-mutant cases. (PubMed Central)
Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole) reduce peripheral estrogen → less ERα activation → loss of ER transcriptional program (estrogen response signatures fall) → growth suppression in ER+ tumours.
Anastrozole directly inhibits aromatase (CYP19A1), reducing conversion of androgens→estrogens → decreased steroid biosynthesis flux and tumour estrogen supply.

PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation provides ER-independent proliferative/survival signalling and is a common escape mechanism from estrogen deprivation; PI3K pathway activation correlates with AI resistance and combining PI3K/mTOR inhibitors can re-sensitize.
Upregulation or activation of RTKs (EGFR/HER2) stimulates downstream PI3K/MAPK signalling, bypassing ER blockade to support proliferation → associated with endocrine resistance.
MAPK (RAS→RAF→MEK→ERK) downstream of RTKs can drive cell-cycle and survival independent of ER; MAPK activation is observed in AI-resistant models and mediates growth despite estrogen deprivation.

Anastrozole has been shown to increase FASN protein (via decreased ubiquitin-mediated degradation) in resistant models; high FASN correlates with worse outcome on anastrozole and can support growth/metabolic rewiring.

Several studies show interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) are constitutively upregulated in AI-resistant models (e.g., IFITM1, PLSCR1); in some contexts suppression of chronic ISG signalling can re-sensitize cells to estradiol-induced apoptosis. So IFN/ISG ↑ is associated with resistance biology in many reports — the relationship with immune activation is complex and context dependent.

IL-6 / STAT3 signalling promotes survival, invasion and can reprogram ER enhancers; IL-6/STAT3 activation has been implicated in endocrine resistance and metastasis — elevated IL-6/JAK-STAT often correlates with poorer response to endocrine therapy.
NF-κB activity can be released when ER is inhibited (ER↔NFκB antagonism); NF-κB drives inflammatory/prosurvival genes and has been repeatedly linked to endocrine resistance.
Effective estrogen suppression causes G1 arrest (↓Cyclin D/CDK4/6 activity) → reduced E2F activity and S-phase gene expression (E2F targets fall). However, **E2F ↑ is a marker of

A high IFN-γ gene signature at baseline reflects a pre-existing antitumor immune response with increased MHC expression, chemokines and PD-L1 induction. Across tumors and in TNBC neoadjuvant/biomarker work, IFN-γ–related mRNA profiles predict better response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, including atezolizumab-containing regimens. (PMC)

The “allograft rejection” set captures cytotoxic CD8⁺ T-cell/NK infiltration and Th1-type inflammation. Such T-cell-inflamed signatures correlate with higher response rates to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors and are incorporated into immune-related gene signatures predicting atezo benefit in TNBC. (AACR Journals)

Baseline activation of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis (especially PD-L1 expression on tumor-infiltrating immune cells) provides the pharmacologic target for atezolizumab. In IMpassion130, clinical benefit was restricted to PD-L1+ mTNBC, supporting that an “on” PD-1/PD-L1 pathway predicts sensitivity. (New England Journal of Medicine)

Tumor-intrinsic Wnt/β-catenin activation is linked to non-T-cell-inflamed, immune-excluded tumors with loss of dendritic-cell recruitment and poor CD8⁺ infiltration, leading to primary resistance to ICIs. Although much data are from melanoma and other cancers, this immune-excluded program is relevant to breast TNBC. (Frontiers)

High TGF-β and EMT signatures define an immune-excluded phenotype with dense stroma and peritumoral T-cell trapping. In atezolizumab-treated urothelial cancer and in TNBC biomarker studies, stromal TGF-β signaling is associated with poor response, while TGF-β blockade plus anti-PD-L1 restores intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and antitumor activity. (PMC)

Downregulation or loss of antigen processing/presentation (e.g., B2M, HLA-I, TAP defects, or JAK/IFN signaling mutations) prevents CD8⁺ T cells from recognizing tumor cells, causing primary or acquired resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade irrespective of PD-L1 status. This mechanism is described across cancers and is relevant to breast. (New England Journal of Medicine)

High LAG-3 on intratumoral T cells marks deeper exhaustion; co-expression with PD-1 defines dysfunctional T cells that respond poorly to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade alone. Upregulation of LAG-3 after PD-1/PD-L1 therapy is a recognized adaptive resistance mechanism, motivating dual PD-1/LAG-3 blockade. (PMC)

PTEN loss and oncogenic PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation promote an immunosuppressive TME via reduced CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and increased VEGF/cytokines. Across cancers (including breast/TNBC), PTEN/PI3K alterations are linked to poorer response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and are being targeted to re-sensitize tumors to ICIs. (MDPI)

Hypoxia via HIF-1α drives VEGF-mediated abnormal vasculature, T-cell exclusion, recruitment of Tregs/MDSCs and PD-L1 upregulation on tumor and myeloid cells. High hypoxia signatures associate with immune-excluded, ICI-refractory tumors, including breast, and VEGF/HIF-1α targeting is being explored to improve PD-1/PD-L1 responses. (SpringerLink)

HRD/BRCA1/2-mutated and HRD-like TNBC have increased genomic instability, higher TMB and more neoantigens, which can favor T-cell infiltration and PD-L1 expression. Multiple reviews link DDR defects to improved ICI benefit, though responses are heterogeneous and depend on co-existing immune-suppressive programs. (PubMed)

IDO1 catabolizes tryptophan to kynurenine, suppressing T-cell proliferation and promoting Tregs and dysfunctional NK cells. High IDO1 expression is common in high-grade/TNBC and often co-expressed with PD-L1, contributing to resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy; IDO1 inhibition (e.g., GDC-0919) has been combined with atezolizumab in early trials. (ScienceDirect)

Effective CD8⁺ T-cell priming requires TCR plus CD28–CD80/86 co-stimulation and IL-2 signaling. In the absence of these signals (e.g., low CD80/86 on APCs, chronic CTLA-4 engagement, steroids), T cells become anergic or exhausted and cannot be fully re-activated by PD-L1 blockade alone, limiting atezo benefit even if PD-L1 is high. (PMC)

Breast tumors with high VEGF-A expression, VEGFR2 and microvessel density are strongly dependent on pathological angiogenesis. Bevacizumab neutralizes VEGF-A, normalizes/prunes vessels and limits perfusion; trials and biomarker studies in HER2-negative MBC and neoadjuvant settings indicate tumors with greater vascular density/angiogenic gene signatures derive more benefit from bevacizumab-containing regimens.

High HIF-1α and hypoxia signatures in breast cancer correlate with VEGF expression, aggressive biology and poor prognosis. In refractory breast cancer, bevacizumab can induce acute hypoxia with secretion of pro-angiogenic and pro-invasive cytokines, leading to early progression. Tumors already hypoxic at baseline are primed for this HIF-driven escape, so bevacizumab is less effective.

EMT activation (loss of E-cadherin; upregulation of TWIST, SNAIL, vimentin) promotes invasion, metastasis and use of vessel co-option rather than sprouting angiogenesis. EMT-high breast tumors are less dependent on VEGF-driven neovascularization and more tolerant of hypoxia, so VEGF-A blockade with bevacizumab yields limited, often transient benefit and can select for more invasive clones.

Notch (including DLL4–Notch) is a key regulator of tip/stalk endothelial cell fate and vessel maturation, and in tumor cells maintains stem-like properties. When Notch signaling is high at baseline, vessels and cancer stem cells can be supported in a relatively VEGF-independent manner. Anti-angiogenic resistance literature highlights Notch upregulation as a canonical escape pathway from VEGF blockade, implying bevacizumab will be less effective in Notch-high tumors (largely cross-cancer but mechanistically applicable to breast cancer).

Breast cancer stem-like cells (ALDH1^high, CD44^+/CD24^−, basal-like transcriptional programs) reside in hypoxic niches, exhibit high self-renewal, and are resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy. HIF-driven pathways promote the breast CSC phenotype. Tumors enriched in these populations at baseline can survive anti-angiogenic stress and re-seed the tumor after bevacizumab, leading to poor and short-lived responses.

In breast cancer, particularly in obesity-associated disease, high baseline FGF2 and FGFR signaling provide an alternative pro-angiogenic axis. Clinical and preclinical work from Jain’s group shows obesity promotes resistance to anti-VEGF therapy via upregulation of IL-6 and FGF2; blocking IL-6 or FGF2 restores sensitivity. Thus, an FGF2/FGFR-high baseline indicates that angiogenesis can be sustained despite VEGF-A neutralization by bevacizumab.

High baseline Ang2 and Tie2 (and Ang2^+ vessel density) in breast cancer correlate with lymph-node invasion, poorer survival and adverse outcomes in trials that included bevacizumab. Ang2 destabilizes vessels and recruits Tie2^+ macrophages, enabling vascular remodeling and immune suppression; persistent or rebound Ang2 undermines VEGF-A blockade. Thus, an Ang2/Tie2-high baseline is a marker of poor bevacizumab benefit.

c-MET activation in breast cancer stimulates MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT3, drives EMT and invasion, and is associated with poor prognosis. Resistance-mechanism reviews identify HGF/c-MET as a key bypass route in tumors resistant to anti-VEGF therapy: under hypoxia, MET signaling is further induced and supports invasive escape and alternative angiogenesis. Baseline MET-high tumors are therefore less likely to respond durably to bevacizumab.

Breast tumors with high baseline TILs and T-cell inflammatory signatures (e.g., many TNBCs) can benefit from vascular normalization: bevacizumab transiently reduces Ang2^+ vasculature, lowers hypoxia and interstitial pressure, and markedly increases CD4⁺/CD8⁺ T-cell and mature dendritic-cell infiltration. This suggests a T-cell–inflamed baseline microenvironment is favorable for bevacizumab-mediated immune enhancement and synergy with chemotherapy or ICIs.

IL-6/STAT3 signaling drives a pro-angiogenic, immunosuppressive milieu through VEGF/FGF2 induction and recruitment of myeloid cells. In obesity-associated breast cancer, high baseline IL-6 and FGF2 levels were strongly associated with resistance to anti-VEGF therapy; IL-6 blockade normalized vessels and restored sensitivity in mouse models. Thus, an IL-6/STAT3-high baseline is a negative predictive factor for bevacizumab.

A high “angiogenesis” gene signature (e.g., VEGF, ANGPTL4, PECAM1, endothelial markers) at baseline indicates that tumor growth is tightly coupled to neovascularization. Breast cancer gene-expression studies and tissue-based angiogenesis markers show that angiogenesis-high tumors (high MVD/angiogenic profile) are more likely to benefit from bevacizumab-containing therapy than angiogenesis-low tumors.

When alternative pro-angiogenic pathways (FGF2/FGFR, PDGFs, Ang2, PlGF) are low at baseline, VEGF-A is the dominant driver of angiogenesis. In this “VEGF-addicted but FGF/Ang2-quiet” setting, bevacizumab shuts down the main angiogenic axis and there are few bypass options, leading to better and more durable responses. This is essentially the inverse of biomarker profiles where high FGF2 or Ang2 predicts poor anti-VEGF benefit.

HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancers with PI3K/AKT1/PTEN alterations show greater benefit from capivasertib + fulvestrant vs fulvestrant alone; presurgical dosing shows strong pAKT and Ki-67 suppression in AKT-addicted ER+ tumours, consistent with oncogene addiction to this pathway.

In PIK3CA- or PTEN-altered ER+ models, capivasertib efficacy is FOXO3-dependent; FOXO3A deletion reduces response and is accompanied by FOXM1 upregulation, whereas preserved FOXO3 enables cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis after AKT inhibition.

Long-term AKT inhibition (including capivasertib) induces FOXM1 upregulation; FOXM1 overexpression attenuates capivasertib’s anti-proliferative effects, while FOXM1 knockdown restores sensitivity, so high FOXM1/E2F/G2M programme marks cells that continue cycling under AKT blockade.

PI3K/AKT pathway inhibition frequently triggers feedback activation of RTKs and ERK, providing an alternative growth and survival route; elevated MAPK signatures or driver alterations decrease dependence on AKT and limit benefit from AKT inhibitors unless co-targeted.

Breast cancer cell lines with high SGK1 show innate resistance to AKT inhibitors (including AZD5363/capivasertib); SGK1 knockdown selectively impairs growth of AKT-inhibitor-resistant cells, and SGK1 can maintain mTORC1 via TSC2 even when AKT is blocked.

Short-term biomarker studies show that incomplete suppression of mTORC1 and translational output despite AKT inhibition is associated with weaker anti-proliferative effects; SGK1–TSC2–mTORC1 signalling can maintain protein synthesis independently of AKT.

Capivasertib trials are in ER+/HER2− disease where ER signalling is active at baseline; FAKTION and CAPItello-291 show improved PFS with capivasertib + fulvestrant, particularly in tumours harbouring PI3K/AKT1/PTEN alterations, consistent with ER-driven tumours relying on both ER and PI3K–AKT survival axes which can be co-targeted.

FOXO3A loss-of-function in PIK3CA-altered ER+ models blunts capivasertib-induced cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis; low FOXO3 or impaired FOXO3 nuclear signalling removes the apoptotic execution arm required for effective killing by AKT inhibition.

When MAPK/RTK pathways are low or co-targeted, tumours become more dependent on PI3K–AKT; preclinical breast models show enhanced anti-tumour activity with capivasertib plus anti-HER2 or MEK/RTK inhibitors, consistent with removal of bypass routes and greater vulnerability to AKT blockade.

In breast tumors where dostarlimab is considered (e.g. TNBC, dMMR, TMB-high), the PD-1/PD-L1 axis is typically engaged: PD-1 is expressed on exhausted TILs and PD-L1 on tumor and myeloid cells. Dostarlimab (anti-PD-1 IgG4) binds PD-1 and blocks PD-L1/PD-L2, releasing this inhibitory brake and restoring T-cell cytotoxicity. Baseline PD-L1 expression and TIL-rich TNBC are associated with benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.

A functional, clonally expanded T-cell repertoire with active TCR signaling and costimulation (CD28, ICOS) underlies effective PD-1 blockade. TNBC and other immunogenic breast cancers with high TILs and T-cell–inflamed gene expression signatures respond better to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors than immune-cold tumors with poor T-cell infiltration or anergic T cells.

An IFN-γ–driven microenvironment (e.g. upregulation of CXCL9/10, IDO1, HLA class I genes, STAT1 targets) defines “hot” tumors enriched for effector CD8⁺ T cells and is consistently associated with higher response rates to PD-1 blockade, including in TNBC treated with pembrolizumab or atezolizumab. Baseline IFN-γ signatures therefore support dostarlimab sensitivity.

HRD/BRCA-mutated breast cancers accumulate cytosolic DNA, activating cGAS–STING and type-I IFN signaling, which recruits CD8⁺ T cells and promotes an inflamed TME. Preclinical BRCA-deficient TNBC models show that STING activation via DNA damage (e.g. PARP inhibitors) is critical for optimal antitumor immunity and improves response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. High cGAS–STING scores correlate with genomic instability and immune cell infiltration in BC.

If baseline antigen presentation is lost, CD8⁺ T cells cannot recognize and kill tumor cells, even if PD-1 is blocked. Loss-of-function mutations in JAK1/2 or B2M and downregulation of HLA class I components are repeatedly linked to primary or acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade; these mechanisms are described across multiple tumor types and are relevant to breast cancers with low MHC-I expression.

High TGF-β in tumor and stromal compartments promotes EMT, fibrosis, Treg and MDSC accumulation and a strongly immune-excluded phenotype. In preclinical breast cancer and pan-tumor data, TGF-β-high tumors show poor CD8⁺ T-cell penetration and limited benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 blockade; combining TGF-β inhibitors or TGF-β/PD-L1 bispecifics with ICIs can restore intratumoral T cells and antitumor activity.

Activated WNT/β-catenin signaling in tumor cells suppresses recruitment/activation of dendritic cells and leads to non-T-cell-inflamed, CD8-poor TMEs. Across solid tumors, WNT/β-catenin activation correlates with immune exclusion and lack of benefit from ICIs; this mechanism likely contributes to immune-cold basal-like or luminal breast cancers with poor ICI responses.

PTEN loss and PI3K–AKT–mTOR hyperactivation increase PD-L1 and immunosuppressive cytokines, reduce TIL infiltration and drive immune evasion. In TNBC and HR⁺/HER2⁻ breast cancer, PTEN loss is associated with poor prognosis and reduced sensitivity to checkpoint blockade; dual targeting of PI3K and PD-1/PD-L1 is being explored to overcome this resistance.

HAVCR2 (TIM-3) is upregulated on chronically stimulated, exhausted CD8⁺ T cells and on Tregs in many tumors. During PD-1 therapy, TIM-3 expression often increases on PD-1-bound T cells via PI3K/AKT-dependent mechanisms, providing a compensatory inhibitory signal and mediating adaptive resistance to PD-1 blockade. High TIM-3 at baseline or on-treatment in breast-like immune-excluded TMEs is therefore a negative predictor for single-agent dostarlimab.

Tumor and myeloid IDO1 catabolize tryptophan to kynurenine, which suppresses effector T-cell and NK-cell function and promotes Treg differentiation. IDO1 expression is common in high-grade TNBC and frequently co-expressed with PD-L1, supporting an IDO-driven immunosuppressive state that blunts PD-1 blockade. High baseline IDO1 therefore predicts decreased sensitivity to single-agent dostarlimab, motivating IDO1 + PD-1 combination strategies.

Elevated IL-10 (often with TGF-β and other suppressive cytokines) promotes Treg expansion, MDSC function and suppression of antigen-presenting cells, maintaining a “cold” or immune-dysfunctional TME. Such cytokine-high tumors show attenuated benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 blockade; durable responses often require either re-programming of myeloid/cytokine networks or combination strategies.

Anti-PD-1–activated T cells depend on intact IFN-γ–JAK–STAT signaling in tumor cells to upregulate antigen presentation, chemokines and pro-apoptotic programs. Loss-of-function JAK1/2 or IFNγR mutations abolish tumor cell responsiveness to IFN-γ and have been directly linked to primary and acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade in melanoma and dMMR cancers; analogous defects would be expected to confer resistance to dostarlimab in breast tumors.

Elacestrant is an oral SERD that degrades ERα, suppresses ER-regulated transcription, and inhibits growth of ER+/HER2– cell lines and PDXs. Tumors with high baseline estrogen-response signatures (strong ER program, often including ESR1 mutations) remain ER-addicted and derive greater benefit when this program is shut down by elacestrant. EMERALD showed the largest PFS gain in ESR1-mutated, ER-driven tumors, consistent with Up estrogen-response → sensitivity.

This Reactome pathway represents canonical ER target-gene transcription. Elacestrant degrades ER and suppresses estrogen-dependent gene expression in vitro and in ER+ PDX models. Tumors with strong baseline activation of this pathway remain transcriptionally ER-dependent and are more likely to respond when elacestrant extinguishes this program.

KEGG estrogen-signaling integrates ER genomic and non-genomic outputs. In metastatic ER+/HER2– disease, ESR1 mutations maintain or enhance estrogen-signaling despite AIs; EMERALD demonstrated a clinically meaningful PFS improvement with elacestrant vs standard endocrine therapy, particularly in ESR1-mutant tumors, indicating that high estrogen-signaling dependence → elacestrant sensitivity, even in AI-resistant settings.

Multi-omic datasets of endocrine-resistant ER+ breast cancer show that relapsed tumors and resistant clones often have reduced estrogen-response gene-set scores and attenuated ER program, with a shift toward alternative signaling and metabolic pathways; such tumors are less dependent on ER and show poorer response to further endocrine/SERD therapy, including elacestrant.

Elacestrant downregulates cell-cycle regulators and proliferation markers, including E2F-regulated genes, in ER+ and CDK4/6i-resistant models, leading to growth inhibition and cell-cycle arrest. Baseline high E2F-target expression reflects a strongly proliferative, ER-cyclin D–CDK4/6-driven state that elacestrant can partially shut down; such tumors often remain endocrine-dependent despite prior CDK4/6i, so Up E2F → more substrate for elacestrant’s antiproliferative effect (recognizing that very extreme proliferation can also mark more aggressive biology).

Preclinical elacestrant studies show robust suppression of proliferation, reduced Ki-67, and tumor regression in multiple ER+ cell lines and PDXs, including those with prior CDK4/6i exposure. Baseline elevated G2/M and cell-cycle gene expression indicates actively cycling, ER-driven luminal tumors; such tumors provide more proliferative substrate for elacestrant to arrest, so Up G2/M → relative sensitivity, although very aggressive, highly proliferative clones may harbor additional resistance mechanisms.

Hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR (via PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, RTK activation) is a well-established mechanism of endocrine resistance in ER+ MBC. Genomic profiling of endocrine-resistant disease shows frequent PI3K pathway alterations at progression; these lesions provide ER-independent survival signals and blunt the efficacy of ER-targeted agents, including SERDs. Preclinical data show that combining elacestrant with PI3K or mTOR inhibitors can resensitize such tumors, implying that baseline Up PI3K/AKT/mTOR is a resistance factor for elacestrant monotherapy, partially overcome in rational combinations.

Independent of the mTORC1 subset, global PI3K–Akt activation (PIK3CA mutations, AKT activation, PTEN loss) is repeatedly linked with poor endocrine therapy response and earlier relapse. Clinical and translational series show higher rates of PI3K pathway alterations in endocrine-resistant vs sensitive ER+ tumors; these alterations attenuate dependence on ER, so Up PI3K-Akt → reduced elacestrant benefit relative to PI3K-wild-type disease, though EMERALD still shows some PFS gain in such subgroups.

Upregulated HER2/EGFR/FGFR and broader RTK signaling provides strong mitogenic and survival input that can bypass ER dependence, producing HER2-enriched / Luminal-to-HER2-like phenotypes with poor response to endocrine therapy alone. Multiple preclinical and clinical datasets link RTK activation and FGFR1 amplification to endocrine resistance in ER+ breast cancer; by class extrapolation, tumors with high RTK signaling are less likely to be controlled by elacestrant monotherapy, and typically require combination strategies (e.g., anti-HER2/FGFR + SERD).

Estrogen signaling promotes survival by modulating pro- and anti-apoptotic gene expression; endocrine therapies and SERDs are most effective when ER+ cells are primed for apoptosis. Transcriptomic studies show that endocrine-resistant ER+ tumors frequently exhibit increased survival signaling and reduced pro-apoptotic gene expression. Consequently, baseline low HALLMARK_APOPTOSIS activity (strong anti-apoptotic bias) is expected to correlate with poor ability to execute cell death after ER degradation, i.e. relative resistance to elacestrant, even if ER signaling is biochemically suppressed.

In NTRK-fusion–positive breast cancers (most commonly secretory carcinoma with ETV6–NTRK3, but also rare non-secretory cases), the TRK pathway is constitutively activated and functions as the dominant oncogenic driver. Entrectinib potently inhibits TRKA/B/C and leads to high, durable response rates in NTRK-fusion solid tumors, including breast, when TRK signaling is active and untreated.

If an NTRK-fusion breast tumor also harbors activating RAS/MAPK lesions (e.g., KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutations, MEK1 alterations) or a high KRAS/MAPK signature, the tumor can maintain ERK signaling independent of TRK, blunting the effect of entrectinib. Convergent MAPK activation is a well-described resistance mechanism to TRK inhibition in multi-tumor series and in entrectinib-treated models; the same biology would predict primary/early resistance if present at baseline in breast cancer.

When the PI3K–AKT–mTOR axis is not already activated by independent genomic events, the tumor is more reliant on NTRK → PI3K/AKT signaling. Entrectinib then effectively shuts down both MAPK and PI3K branches, favoring apoptosis. Preclinical TRK-driven models show strong pro-apoptotic effects when PI3K/mTOR is not independently activated, and dual TRK + PI3K/mTOR blockade further deepens responses.

MET amplification or overexpression reactivates RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT independent of TRK. MET amplification has been directly documented as a mechanism of acquired resistance to entrectinib in ROS1+ NSCLC, and TRK-i reviews highlight MET as a recurrent bypass node. If such MET activation exists at baseline in an NTRK-fusion breast tumor, entrectinib monotherapy is unlikely to produce deep or durable responses.

Tumors with intact apoptotic machinery can rapidly execute apoptosis once TRK signaling is shut off. In TRK-inhibitor models, responders show strong induction of cleaved caspases and apoptosis gene signatures after treatment; the clinical pattern of deep, rapid regressions in many NTRK-fusion tumors is consistent with this “primed” state. Baseline apoptotic competence is therefore a positive modifier of entrectinib sensitivity.

EMT-high states generally correlate with reduced dependence on a single RTK, lower proliferation, increased drug-tolerant persisters, and activation of alternative RTKs (AXL, FGFR, MET). TRK-resistance reviews list EMT and lineage plasticity as non-genetic resistance mechanisms; although most data are from other tumor types, an EMT-high signature in NTRK-fusion breast cancer would plausibly predict shallower or shorter responses to entrectinib.

In a HER2-positive breast cancer that also carries an NTRK fusion, HER2 amplification often remains the dominant driver of PI3K/MAPK signaling. In such a setting, TRK inhibition alone may not fully suppress downstream growth pathways; clinically, HER2-addicted tumors generally require HER2-directed therapy. Thus, baseline high HER2 activity is expected to blunt the benefit of entrectinib monotherapy, unless HER2 is co-inhibited. Evidence is extrapolated from multi-driver RTK settings and tumor-agnostic TRK-i series rather than from large NTRK+ HER2+ BC cohorts.

Hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR via PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, or RTK activation drives proliferation and endocrine resistance in HR+/HER2− and some TNBC tumors. Everolimus (mTORC1 inhibitor) is most effective when the tumor is addicted to this axis; low-activity PI3K/AKT/mTOR tumors derive less benefit. (PubMed)

High mTORC1 output (p-S6K, p-4EBP1) marks tumors with strong translational drive and cell-cycle progression. Everolimus directly inhibits mTORC1; tumors with elevated baseline p-S6K/4EBP1 show greater growth suppression, while those with weak mTORC1 activity or activating mTOR mutations that blunt inhibition are less responsive. (Nature)

Tumors with a strong estrogen-response signature (HALLMARK_ESTROGEN_RESPONSE) are ER-driven and depend on ER signaling for growth. In this setting, everolimus plus endocrine therapy improves PFS by blocking mTORC1-mediated escape from endocrine therapy and by downregulating ER expression/activity. ER-negative or ER-pathway-low tumors show minimal benefit. (PubMed)

High E2F target expression (Cyclin E, DNA-replication genes, high Ki-67) indicates rapidly proliferating, mTORC1-dependent tumors. Everolimus causes G1 arrest and reduces E2F target expression; thus, tumors with high baseline proliferation signatures tend to have greater cell-cycle arrest and clinical benefit, whereas indolent/low-E2F tumors gain less. (Physiology Journals)

mTORC1 normally suppresses autophagy. Tumors with high basal autophagy or strong autophagy induction under everolimus can recycle nutrients and clear damaged components, surviving mTORC1 blockade. Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy (e.g., Beclin-1, LC3 modulation or agents like melittin) re-sensitizes breast-cancer cells to everolimus, supporting “autophagy-high” as a resistance state. (Physiology Journals)

Everolimus-resistant ER+ and long-term estrogen-deprived models frequently show MYC upregulation and dependency. High MYC or MYC-target signatures allow maintenance of growth and metabolism even when mTORC1 is inhibited. MYC inhibition or suppression re-sensitizes these cells to mTOR inhibitors, and high MYC expression in metastatic breast cancer correlates with poor response to everolimus. (PMC)

Everolimus selectively inhibits mTORC1 but spares mTORC2. When upstream RTKs (IGF1R, EGFR, HER2/HER3) or PI3K are strongly active, mTORC1 inhibition relieves feedback, leading to AKT hyperactivation via mTORC2 and other routes. Tumors with strong RTK/AKT signaling at baseline or that rapidly ramp up AKT under therapy tend to maintain survival signaling and show clinical or acquired resistance to everolimus. (Wikipedia)

Tumors with high STAT3 → HIF-1α → VEGF signaling are highly vascular and rely on pathological angiogenesis. Everolimus downregulates this axis, reducing VEGF production, microvessel density and, in some models, lymphangiogenesis. Angiogenesis-high tumors therefore have more “room” for everolimus to exert anti-angiogenic and growth-suppressive effects; where VEGF/HIF signaling is low or bypassed by alternative angiogenic pathways, this mechanism contributes less and resistance is more likely. (PMC)

In TNBC 4T1 models, everolimus monotherapy inhibited mTOR signaling but increased PD-L1 expression on intratumoral endothelial cells, reduced CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and failed to control tumor growth. Combination with PD-1 blockade normalized vasculature, restored CD8⁺ infiltration, and overcame this resistance. Baseline or therapy-induced high PD-L1 and an immune-cold microenvironment therefore align with poor response to everolimus alone but may define candidates for everolimus + ICI combinations. (PubMed)

ER+ breast tumors selected for Exemestane typically show active peripheral/intratumoral estrogen biosynthesis via aromatase (CYP19A1). High estrogen production makes the tumor dependent on this axis; irreversible aromatase blockade by Exemestane depletes estrogen and suppresses growth.

Classical AI-sensitive tumors rely on ligand-dependent ERα signaling: high ER expression and ER-regulated transcription drive proliferation. Depriving estrogen with Exemestane shuts down this ESR pathway. ESR1 activating mutations or loss of ER reduce AI benefit and drive resistance.

Broad estrogen signaling (genomic nuclear ER and rapid non-genomic membrane ER effects) is typically active in hormone-dependent tumors. Exemestane indirectly suppresses both arms by lowering estrogen levels; high baseline estrogen signaling therefore predicts benefit.

In postmenopausal HR+ breast cancer, steroid hormone metabolism is skewed toward local estrone/estradiol production from adrenal precursors. High activity of this estrogenic branch provides substrate for ER signaling and makes tumors more susceptible to aromatase inhibition with Exemestane.

Upregulated EGFR/HER2→MAPK signaling provides a ligand-independent growth/survival route that bypasses ER. In Exemestane-resistant models, Exemestane induces AREG, which stimulates EGFR–MAPK and sustains proliferation despite estrogen depletion; clinically, HER2/EGFR activation is a key endocrine-resistance mechanism.

Constitutive PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation (PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, RTK activation) uncouples proliferation and survival from ER/estrogen, leading to intrinsic or acquired resistance to aromatase inhibitors. This underpins clinical benefit from combining endocrine therapy with mTOR (everolimus) or PI3K/AKT inhibitors in HR+ disease.

AR is co-expressed in ~70–80% of ER+ cancers and frequently marks luminal, lower-grade, endocrine-responsive disease. In this setting, moderate AR activity can antagonize ER-driven proliferation and is associated with better prognosis, although high AR/ER ratios or specific contexts can also contribute to resistance. Overall, AR-positive luminal tumors are generally suitable for AI therapy.

High G2M/E2F/Ki67 signatures reflect rapidly proliferating luminal B biology. Such tumors are often less durably controlled by AI monotherapy, show shorter time to treatment failure on AIs, and are more likely to need chemotherapy or combination targeted therapy. Strong down-regulation of this signature after short-term Exemestane is a good PD marker of sensitivity, but baseline high G2M/E2F tends to predict relative endocrine resistance.

The key determinant for AI benefit is capacity to induce apoptosis when ER signaling is withdrawn. In neoadjuvant AI studies, successful endocrine therapy leads to increased apoptotic index together with reduced Ki67; tumors that fail to upregulate apoptosis despite estrogen deprivation show poorer outcomes. Baseline pro-/anti-apoptotic balance is heterogeneous, but therapy-induced Apoptosis↑ is a marker of Exemestane sensitivity.[Up on-treatment (baseline direction not fixed)]

EMT programs (loss of epithelial markers, gain of mesenchymal/stem-like traits) confer invasion, metastatic potential, and broad drug resistance. EMT-high luminal tumors often show reduced ER dependence and worse response to endocrine therapies, including AIs.

Chronic IL-6/JAK/STAT3 and TNF/NFκB signaling promotes a pro-inflammatory, pro-survival microenvironment, enhances stem-like features, and down-modulates ER signaling. Intratumoral inflammation signatures, high STAT3/NFκB activity, and cytokine-rich microenvironments have been linked to endocrine resistance and poorer outcomes in HR+ breast cancer.

Tumors that depend on active ER signaling are more likely to respond to ER degradation by fulvestrant; if ER signaling is already low/down, the tumor is less ER-dependent and fulvestrant is less likely to produce benefit. (PubMed Central)

Activating PIK3CA/PI3K–AKT signaling promotes cell survival and mediates endocrine (including fulvestrant) resistance; combining PI3K inhibitors with fulvestrant shows clinical benefit in PIK3CA-mutant disease. (PubMed)

Upregulated HER family signaling provides bypass survival/proliferation signals and can be induced after ER blockade (fulvestrant can increase ErbB3/HER2 expression), producing resistance unless co-targeted. (PubMed Central)

ERK pathway activation sustains proliferation and can circumvent ER loss; ERK activation correlates with fulvestrant resistance and combining ERK/MEK inhibition can restore sensitivity in models. (PubMed Central)

NF-κB drives expression of anti-apoptotic/pro-survival genes (e.g., BCL2 family); IRF1 induction suppresses NF-κB and promotes fulvestrant-induced apoptosis — active NF-κB therefore promotes resistance. (PubMed Central)
Repression/loss of GPER1 has been linked experimentally to fulvestrant resistance (GPER modulation and epigenetic changes observed in resistant cell models). (PubMed Central)

Upregulation of CDK6 (and/or cyclin D/CDK4/6 axis) enables G1→S progression despite ER loss; high CDK6 correlates with shorter PFS on fulvestrant and combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with fulvestrant is effective clinically. (PubMed)
RB1 loss abrogates the G1 checkpoint and undermines fulvestrant-induced G1 arrest; RB loss is associated with endocrine resistance. (PubMed Central)
IFNγ induces IRF1/STAT1 which suppresses NF-κB and anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and promotes caspase activation — IRF1 activity restores fulvestrant sensitivity in resistant models. (PubMed)
Fulvestrant’s anti-tumor effect in ER+ cells involves induction of caspase-dependent apoptosis (IRF1/BAX/BAK mediated); active apoptotic machinery facilitates drug efficacy. (PubMed Central)

In HER2-amplified breast cancer, ErbB signaling is constitutively **up**, driving MAPK and PI3K/AKT. Lapatinib is indicated exactly in this context: tumors are “addicted” to HER2/EGFR; blocking the kinases collapses downstream signaling and halts proliferation. If ErbB signaling is not upregulated at baseline (non-HER2-driven), lapatinib benefit is limited.

HER2 amplification normally drives **PI3K/AKT/mTOR upregulation**, and HER2-dependent PI3K signaling is successfully switched off by lapatinib in sensitive tumors. However, when PI3K/AKT is hyperactivated by **PIK3CA mutations or PTEN loss**, the pathway can remain active despite HER2 blockade, mediating intrinsic or acquired resistance.

Baseline HER2+ tumors often show high E2F and G1/S gene expression (Cyclin D1, CDK4/6 targets), reflecting rapid proliferation. Lapatinib sensitivity associates with **on-treatment suppression** of these E2F targets. Tumors that already have RB loss or very high CCND1 can bypass HER2-CDK4/6 control and may be less inhibited by lapatinib.

In ER+/HER2+ (“triple-positive”) disease, blocking HER2 can de-repress **FOXO3A-mediated ER transcription**, increasing ER dependence and allowing tumors to survive on ER signaling. High ER signaling at baseline predicts **limited benefit from HER2-only blockade**; adding aromatase inhibitors or SERMs/SERDs improves response.

An autocrine **heregulin (NRG1)–HER3–EGFR–PI3K** axis maintains PI3K/AKT and ERK signaling even when HER2 is inhibited. Baseline high heregulin/HER3 or rapid induction during therapy drives resistance to lapatinib and other EGFR/HER2 TKIs; blocking HER3 or PI3K/mTOR restores sensitivity in models.

GRB7 is frequently co-amplified with HER2. Lapatinib-mediated AKT inhibition can relieve GRB7 repression, further increasing its expression. High GRB7 enhances receptor tyrosine kinase and FAK-driven survival/migration. Knock-down of GRB7 increases lapatinib activity, indicating that **high baseline GRB7 is an adverse, resistance-leaning feature**.

In HER2+ breast tumors, chronic HER2 blockade selects for **AXL-high clones**. AXL activation reinstates MAPK and PI3K signaling independent of HER2, driving proliferation, migration and metastasis despite lapatinib. High baseline AXL or EMT signatures predict **poor response**, and AXL inhibition can re-sensitize cells.

Activated **MET–HGF** signaling provides an alternate RTK driver that maintains PI3K/MAPK activity when HER2 is inhibited. In HER2-amplified breast cancer models, HGF stimulation or MET overexpression reduces lapatinib-induced apoptosis and proliferation arrest; MET inhibition reverses resistance.

In sensitive HER2+ breast cancer cells, lapatinib induces **FOXO3A activation and p27^Kip1 upregulation**, enforcing G1 arrest. Tumors where FOXO3A/p27 are already low or cannot be induced (e.g. miR-221-mediated p27 suppression) show reduced G1 arrest and **lapatinib resistance**. Thus a baseline state where FOXO3A/p27 are **intact and not heavily downregulated** predicts better response.

HER2 signaling feeds into Cyclin D1/CDK4 and RB phosphorylation, driving E2F and proliferation. Lapatinib can suppress Cyclin D1 and induce RB hypophosphorylation in sensitive tumors. However, **RB loss** or very high Cyclin D1/CDK4 activity uncouples cell cycle from HER2, limiting the effect of HER2 TKIs. Thus a typical HER2-addicted, RB-proficient tumor with upregulated Cyclin D1/CDK4 is still **sensitive**, whereas RB-defective or CCND1-amplified tumors are more **resistant**.

Recent work shows lapatinib can **increase mitochondrial respiration and OXPHOS proteins** in HER2+ cells even while inhibiting proliferation, suggesting a metabolic shift toward oxidative ATP production. Lapatinib-resistant cells upregulate metabolic stress and glucose-deprivation response networks, often involving ERRα-regulated oxidative metabolism. Thus a baseline or easily inducible **OXPHOS-high state** is interpreted as a **potential resistance-leaning adaptation**, though this is less validated than RTK-based mechanisms.

In **EGFR-positive TNBC** models (HER2-negative), lapatinib paradoxically activates **NF-κB and COX-2**, increasing motility and metastasis; NF-κB activation can be exploited to sensitize to proteasome inhibitors but does **not** define a good lapatinib monotherapy indication. For standard HER2+ breast cancer, NF-κB status is not a primary biomarker for prescribing lapatinib; in EGFR-driven TNBC with NF-κB-high phenotype, lapatinib alone is unlikely to be beneficial and may be harmful.

PTEN is a major negative regulator of PI3K/AKT. HER2+ breast tumors with **PTEN loss or very low PTEN** maintain AKT phosphorylation even when HER2 is inhibited, leading to impaired response to trastuzumab and HER2 TKIs including lapatinib. Clinically, PTEN-low HER2+ tumors show worse outcomes on HER2-targeted therapy, consistent with **resistance**.

Lapatinib’s durable effect requires not just cell-cycle arrest but also **induction of apoptosis** in HER2+ cells. Tumors with low baseline BIM/BAX or high anti-apoptotic molecules (BCL-2, BCL-xL, survivin) show attenuated apoptosis on HER2 blockade and develop resistance. Lapatinib-resistant models often exhibit rewired apoptotic signaling; strategies that re-engage apoptosis (e.g., BH3 mimetics, TRAIL agonists) can overcome resistance.

In secretory breast carcinoma (SBC) and rare other NTRK-fusion breast cancers, ETV6–NTRK3 or other NTRK fusions create a constitutively active TRK oncoprotein that drives proliferation and survival. Larotrectinib selectively inhibits TRKA/B/C, shutting down this pathway and producing high response rates irrespective of tumor histology.

Activated TRK receptors signal to PI3K–AKT–mTOR, promoting survival and resistance to apoptosis. In TRK-fusion models, larotrectinib acutely suppresses phospho-AKT/mTOR and induces tumor regression. However, many non-NTRK-driven breast cancers also have high PI3K/AKT, so this hallmark alone should not be used as a prescribing biomarker for larotrectinib.

TRK activation engages the RAS/MAPK cascade, driving proliferation. Preclinical TRK-fusion models show that larotrectinib inhibits downstream ERK phosphorylation together with PI3K/AKT, consistent with addiction of the MAPK arm to TRK signaling. However, MAPK activation is ubiquitous in breast cancer and is not specific for NTRK fusions.

Oncogenic TRK signaling promotes cell survival and inhibits apoptosis. In TRK-fusion models and clinical biopsies, TRK inhibition (including larotrectinib) leads to increased apoptotic markers and tumor shrinkage. Nevertheless, low apoptosis is a general hallmark of malignancy and does not uniquely identify NTRK-fusion-positive breast cancer.

Letrozole suppresses aromatase → lowers estrogen → turns off ER-target genes and reduces proliferation. Tumors with high “estrogen response” gene-set scores tend to have better outcomes on endocrine therapy, because they are truly estrogen-driven; loss of estrogen response or ligand-independent signaling is a resistance feature. (PMC)

Letrozole is a potent non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor; it works best when tumor growth depends on local estrogen synthesis from androgens. High aromatase/steroidogenesis provides a clear pharmacologic target; if estrogen biosynthesis is already low and ER signaling is ligand-independent, AI benefit is attenuated. (PMC)

ER-positive tumors that respond to neoadjuvant letrozole show marked early reductions in Ki67 and cell-cycle gene expression; low residual proliferation after short-term letrozole predicts good outcome. By contrast, tumors that maintain high E2F4/FOXM1/PLK1-driven proliferation despite estrogen deprivation are resistant. So baseline Up indicates endocrine-driven proliferation (targetable), but failure to downregulate cell-cycle programs on AI marks resistance. (PMC)

Activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR promotes survival and growth despite estrogen deprivation and is repeatedly associated with endocrine (including AI) resistance. High AKT activity confers resistance to letrozole in preclinical models, and multiple clinical/biological datasets link pathway activation to ET failure and justify PI3K/mTOR inhibitors as combination partners with AIs. (Annals of Oncology)

Growth-factor signaling via MAPK/ERK provides a parallel proliferation axis that can maintain cyclin D–CDK4/6 activity even when ER signaling is blocked. Clinical and preclinical data tie hyperactive MAPK (often with HER2 or FGFR cross-talk) to luminal B biology, higher proliferation, and reduced endocrine responsiveness. Letrozole may transiently reduce ER-driven MAPK, but tumors that maintain or re-activate MAPK/ERK tend to be resistant. (ScienceDirect)

Most breast tumors exhibit suppressed apoptosis (high BCL-2/BCL-XL etc.). Effective estrogen deprivation shifts the balance toward apoptosis and/or senescence in ER-dependent cells. Letrozole-sensitive tumors show antiproliferative effects and can undergo apoptosis; resistant tumors often have survival pathway activation (e.g. PI3K/AKT, HIF-1α, etc.) that maintains anti-apoptotic signaling so they fail to die despite ER blockade. Baseline apoptosis per se is less predictive than the ability to increase apoptosis on treatment. (PMC)

FOXM1 is a master regulator of cell-cycle progression, proliferation, and metastasis; it is overexpressed in many breast cancers, and high FOXM1 is strongly associated with resistance to endocrine therapies. Functional data show that FOXM1 drives stem-like, invasive, therapy-resistant states, and that FOXM1 or its network is enriched in tumors resistant to prolonged neoadjuvant letrozole. (PMC)

PLK1 is a key mitotic kinase closely linked to FOXM1 and high Ki67. Kinome-wide screens and expression analyses show that PLK1 activity correlates with hormone-independent proliferation; PLK1 and FOXM1 transcripts are co-upregulated in hormone-independent and endocrine-resistant tumors. Pathway enrichment in letrozole non-responders identifies PLK1-associated signaling as activated. (PMC)

SDC1 is a heparan-sulfate proteoglycan involved in cell–matrix interaction, growth-factor presentation, EMT, and stem-like phenotypes. It is often overexpressed in ER-negative, highly proliferative breast cancers, and is linked to metastasis and therapy resistance across tumor types. In ER⁺ disease, SDC1 can modulate IL6/STAT3 and EGFR pathways, potentially fostering endocrine escape, but specific clinical data tying SDC1 upregulation to letrozole failure are sparse → treat as plausible but cross-context extrapolation. (Frontiers)

MMP2 and MMP9 (gelatinases) promote basement-membrane degradation, invasion and metastasis, and are commonly upregulated in advanced breast cancer. Letrozole has been shown to decrease MMP2/9 expression and proliferation in ER⁺ MCF-7 cells, consistent with an anti-invasive effect; clinical AI studies show differential modulation of MMPs across AIs. Thus high ECM/MMP activity at baseline marks aggressive biology; failure to suppress (or re-induction of) MMP/ECM programs under letrozole supports a resistant phenotype. (PubMed)

Breast tumors commonly show increased angiogenesis driven by HIF-1α and VEGF. High HIF/VEGF signaling is linked to poor prognosis and therapy resistance in breast cancer. Letrozole can reduce HIF-1α and phospho-mTOR expression in tumors, and regression of estrogen-dependent disease will secondarily lower angiogenic drive. Baseline strongly pro-angiogenic, hypoxic tumors are typically more aggressive and relatively endocrine-refractory; normalizing or reducing angiogenesis on letrozole aligns with sensitivity. (JCI)

HIF-1α overexpression is associated with drug resistance, higher risk of metastasis, and poor outcomes in breast cancer. Mechanistically, HIF-1α drives glycolysis, angiogenesis, EMT, survival pathways and drug efflux. Letrozole can downregulate HIF-1α and phospho-mTOR in ER⁺ tumors, but basal and therapy-driven HIF-1α activity generally marks a more resistant phenotype rather than a protective one. So the corrected view is Up = resistance, contrary to the original table. (Frontiers)

In ER⁺/HER2⁻ neoadjuvant letrozole trials, an increase in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes during AI therapy correlated with poorer antiproliferative response and lack of clinical benefit, unlike the good-prognosis association seen in TNBC. Transcriptomic profiling of AI-treated ER⁺ tumors also identifies immune-high, estrogen-low phenotypes with less endocrine responsiveness. Thus, in the luminal AI context, immune/TIL-high (or rising TIL) signatures tend to mark endocrine resistance and might instead flag candidates for combined ET + CDK4/6i or ET + immunotherapy. (PubMed)

HER2⁺ breast cancers that are candidates for margetuximab typically have amplified/overexpressed HER2 and active ErbB signaling. Margetuximab binds the same HER2 epitope as trastuzumab and preserves its anti-proliferative blockade of HER2–PI3K/MAPK signaling while enhancing Fc-dependent effector functions. Thus, high baseline ErbB/HER2 activity indicates pathway dependence and supports sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibodies, including margetuximab.

This gene set captures the oncogenic HER2 signaling module. In HER2-amplified tumors, high ERBB2 signaling marks HER2 addiction and is associated with benefit from HER2-targeted monoclonal antibodies. Margetuximab maintains the HER2-blocking, anti-proliferative mechanism while adding Fc-optimization, so a high ERBB2 signaling signature at baseline is expected to correspond to sensitivity to margetuximab, as it does for trastuzumab and related agents.

This pathway comprises c-Cbl–mediated ubiquitination, internalization and degradation of HER2 and associated downregulation modules. High enrichment of this “downregulation of ERBB2 signaling” gene set at baseline may reflect chronic prior HER2-targeted exposure with reduced surface HER2 and weakened HER2 addiction. Such tumors may rely more on alternative pathways (e.g., PI3K or other RTKs), leading to reduced incremental benefit from another HER2 IgG1 (margetuximab), although this is inferred from general HER2 biology rather than prospectively validated for this exact gene set.

In HER2⁺ BC, constitutive activation of PI3K–AKT–mTOR via PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss or other alterations is a well-described mechanism of reduced response to trastuzumab and other HER2-targeted therapies, with multiple neoadjuvant and retrospective studies showing lower pCR and poorer outcomes when the PI3K pathway is activated. Since margetuximab shares the same HER2-blocking mechanism but adds Fc-engineering, baseline high PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling is expected to attenuate sensitivity to margetuximab as well (Fc optimization may not fully overcome oncogenic PI3K signaling).

Margetuximab is Fc-engineered to increase affinity for activating FcγRIIIa (CD16A) and decrease binding to inhibitory FcγRIIb (CD32B), thereby enhancing NK-cell–mediated ADCC compared with trastuzumab. A tumor/microenvironment with robust NK-cell presence and intact NK cytotoxicity machinery (reflected by higher NK-cell signatures or NK-cytotoxicity pathways) is expected to be more sensitive to margetuximab because it can better exploit its Fc-optimized ADCC.

This Reactome pathway provides mechanistic granularity for FcγR-dependent uptake and killing of antibody-coated cells. Because margetuximab is specifically engineered to bias signaling towards activating FcγRs, a higher baseline capacity for FcγR-dependent phagocytosis (appropriate myeloid cell populations and signaling) should favor sensitivity to margetuximab through enhanced ADCP in addition to NK-cell ADCC.

High IFN-γ gene-set enrichment represents a Th1-type, T/NK-cell–inflamed TME. Such “hot” tumors are generally more responsive to immune-mediated mechanisms, including checkpoint inhibitors and Fc-dependent effector functions. Fc-engineered antibodies like margetuximab can boost NK-driven IFN-γ production, and preclinical/clinical combinations of anti-HER2 mAbs with PD-1 inhibitors (e.g. margetuximab + pembrolizumab in HER2⁺ tumors) are built on this biology. Direct BC data for this exact hallmark as a biomarker are limited, so this is a mechanistically plausible but not formally validated sensitivity marker.

HER2-amplified / HER2-mutant tumors have upregulated ERBB2 signalling and are “HER2-addicted”. Neratinib is an irreversible pan-HER TKI (HER1/2/4); high baseline HER2 signalling is required for benefit and predicts sensitivity, provided there is no dominant downstream bypass (e.g. TORC1, PI3K). (PMC)

HER2 overexpression activates RAS→RAF→MEK→ERK. Neratinib suppresses HER2 and reduces pERK, producing growth arrest in HER2-dependent models. However, MAPK Up due to RAS/RAF mutations or alternative RTKs can maintain ERK signalling despite HER2 blockade and drive resistance. (PMC)

Activating PIK3CA mutations or PTEN loss cause hyperactive PI3K/AKT signalling that can sustain growth even when HER2 is inhibited. In HER2+ breast cancer, PIK3CA mutations are repeatedly associated with lower pCR and reduced benefit from HER2-targeted regimens, and this is widely considered a resistance mechanism also relevant to neratinib. (PMC)

Sudhan et al. show that TORC1/mTORC1 hyperactivation drives neratinib resistance; PDX and cell-line models with high pS6/p4EBP1 are neratinib-resistant and can be resensitized by TORC1 inhibition (everolimus). By inference, tumors without marked mTORC1 hyperactivation (i.e. relatively lower TORC1 at baseline) remain more HER2-dependent and are more likely to be neratinib-sensitive. (PubMed)

Neratinib clearly induces G1 arrest and reduces Cyclin D1/CDK4/6/E2F signalling in HER2-dependent models. Tumors that lack strong, autonomous cell-cycle deregulation (no RB loss, no massive CCND1/CDK4/6 hyperactivation) and rely mainly on HER2 for proliferation are more likely to be controlled by HER2 TKIs. A relatively lower baseline G2M/E2F score in a HER2-amplified tumor can be viewed as a favourable, but low-evidence feature. (PMC)

Neratinib induces apoptosis in HER2-dependent cancer cells (caspase activation, PARP cleavage). Tumors that are “apoptotically primed” (higher pro-apoptotic signalling / lower anti-apoptotic buffering) are more likely to undergo cell death once HER2 and its downstream survival signals are blocked, so a higher apoptosis gene-set at baseline is a plausible (though not yet validated) sensitivity feature. (PMC)

In HR+/HER2+ or HER2-low BC, strong ER signalling can sustain proliferation when HER2 is inhibited, contributing to suboptimal response to HER2-directed therapy alone. Preclinical and emerging clinical data support triple combinations (neratinib + endocrine therapy + CDK4/6i) to overcome this. Thus, baseline estrogen-response Up is unfavourable for neratinib alone, but compatible with sensitivity when combined with appropriate endocrine ± CDK4/6 blockade. (Nature)

HER2-negative breast cancers with germline/somatic BRCA1/2 mutations or other HRR defects show homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). PARP1 inhibition and PARP-trapping create lesions that HRD cells cannot repair, leading to synthetic lethality and clear clinical benefit with olaparib (e.g., OlympiAD, OlympiA).

In BRCA1-deficient mammary tumors, loss of 53BP1/RIF1/Shieldin downregulates classical NHEJ and allows DNA end-resection and RAD51 loading, functionally restoring HRR and abrogating PARPi synthetic lethality. A BRCA1-mutant breast tumor with 53BP1/Shieldin-low NHEJ at baseline is therefore predicted to be less responsive to olaparib.

When PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling is low or blocked (e.g. by PI3K inhibitors or other upstream blockade), BRCA1/2 expression and HRR capacity fall, creating a “BRCAness” phenotype in BRCA-wild-type TNBC. Such tumors become more reliant on PARP-mediated repair and are strongly sensitized to PARP inhibition, supporting olaparib (often in combination) in PI3K-low/BRCAness breast tumors.

In BRCA-deficient TNBC models, olaparib-induced cytosolic DNA activates cGAS–STING and type I IFN, driving CD8⁺ T-cell recruitment. Tumors with an already inflamed, IFN-rich microenvironment or strong STING–IFN inducibility show greater dependence on immune-mediated tumor control and respond better to PARPi ± immunotherapy. A baseline IFN-α/IFN-I–high signature therefore supports olaparib sensitivity.

Overexpression of ABC transporters (ABCB1/P-gp, ABCG2, etc.) increases efflux of olaparib, lowering intracellular drug levels. PARPi-resistance models (largely ovarian and prostate but mechanistically applicable) show that ABCB1 upregulation drives cross-resistance to olaparib and taxanes, and ABCB1 inhibition can restore sensitivity; a baseline MDR-high breast tumor is thus predicted to be olaparib-poor-responding.

PARP inhibition increases replication stress and reliance on ATR–CHK1 to pause the cell cycle and coordinate repair. Tumors with high ATR/CHK1 signaling can better stabilise stalled forks and repair damage, promoting survival and olaparib resistance; multiple studies show that ATR/CHK1 inhibition re-sensitises PARPi-resistant cells. Baseline ATR/CHK1-high status therefore predicts reduced olaparib efficacy unless co-targeted.

For olaparib to produce tumor regression, DNA damage must be translated into apoptosis. Breast tumors with intact or heightened p53-dependent and p53-independent apoptotic signaling (e.g. higher BAX/PUMA, lower anti-apoptotic BCL-2) more readily undergo apoptosis after PARPi-induced DNA damage, favouring sensitivity. (Note: many gBRCA/TNBC tumors are TP53-mutant yet still respond; this is a probabilistic, not absolute, relationship.)

TP53 loss, common in TNBC, impairs DNA damage-induced apoptosis and G1/S checkpoint control, facilitating survival under genotoxic stress and enabling clonal evolution (e.g. HR restoration, FA/HR rewiring). While HRD TP53-mutant tumors can still show initial olaparib responses, TP53-deficient clones are more likely to tolerate ongoing damage and develop resistance; so baseline TP53 loss is a risk factor for poorer long-term benefit rather than an absolute contraindication.

FA pathway genes (e.g. FANCA, FANCD2) coordinate repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks and interface with HR. FA-deficient cells are hypersensitive to PARPi and other DNA-damaging agents; FA dysfunction in solid tumors produces an HRD-like state (“BRCAness”), predicting sensitivity to olaparib in breast cancer by the same synthetic-lethal logic as BRCA1/2 loss.

If PARP1 itself is lost or catalytically inactivated in the tumor at baseline, olaparib cannot effectively trap PARP1 on DNA. This “loss of target” reduces PARP-trapping cytotoxicity and is a recognised mechanism of PARPi resistance, albeit often accompanied by some BER defects. Such tumors are predicted to be intrinsically less responsive to olaparib despite DNA repair abnormalities.
Paclitaxel primarily kills actively cycling cells by disrupting mitosis; a higher baseline G2/M program (high proliferation/mitotic entry) generally aligns with greater taxane vulnerability.
Paclitaxel targets microtubule/spindle dynamics; tumors with stronger baseline mitotic-spindle/mitosis activity (many cells entering mitosis) are more likely to be impacted.
Paclitaxel-induced mitotic stress triggers intrinsic apoptosis; taxane exposure can inactivate anti-apoptotic BCL2 via phosphorylation and/or direct interaction, enabling caspase-mediated cell death.

Breast tumors with higher baseline immune activation (including IFN-related gene programs/TIL-associated signatures) frequently show better response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (commonly anthracycline/taxane regimens), consistent with chemo–immune cooperation.
Paclitaxel can activate TLR4 signaling in breast-cancer cells; high baseline TLR4/NF-κB inflammatory-survival wiring aligns with reduced paclitaxel cytotoxicity and more aggressive behavior.
High baseline PI3K/AKT survival signaling counteracts mitotic-stress death programs and is associated with resistance to chemotherapy in breast cancer.

Pro-tumor cytokine loops (e.g., IL6/IL8) can create NF-κB/Wnt–reinforced autocrine feedback, enriching drug-tolerant/CSC-like populations after chemotherapy exposure/withdrawal, supporting resistance.
ABCB1/P-gp and related ABC transporters reduce intracellular paclitaxel levels, a canonical taxane resistance mechanism.
Paclitaxel efficacy depends on cells progressing into mitosis; therefore higher baseline cell-cycle activity (cycling fraction) generally aligns with better response than a quiescent baseline state.

High baseline angiogenesis often co-occurs with inflammatory cytokine/NF-κB programs and can support tumor progression and therapy resistance; paclitaxel–TLR4 inflammatory circuits can also promote angiogenesis/lymphangiogenesis in relevant models.
Palbociclib targets the cyclin D–CDK4/6 → RB → E2F axis; tumors with upregulated cell-cycle/CDK4/6 activity and intact RB are most likely to respond. (PubMed Central)

High baseline E2F-target expression reflects active RB phosphorylation and S-phase entry; CDK4/6 inhibition suppresses E2F-driven transcription, so high E2F dependency predicts vulnerability. (PubMed Central)
Upregulation of G2/M drivers (PLK1, AURKs, WEE1) or cell-cycle plasticity permits bypass of G1 arrest and is a documented mechanism of CDK4/6i resistance. (PubMed Central)
PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation provides pro-survival/proliferative signaling that can bypass CDK4/6 dependence; targeting PI3K/mTOR can restore sensitivity in some models. (PubMed Central)
FGFR1 amplification/activation sustains proliferation and mediates resistance to endocrine + CDK4/6 inhibitors; FGFR inhibition can reverse resistance in preclinical models. (PubMed)
RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK signaling increases cyclin D/E and can reactivate cell-cycle progression independent of CDK4/6, contributing to acquired resistance. (PubMed Central)
c-Myc activation represses miR-29b-3p and elevates CDK6 and other programs; MYC activation correlates with palbociclib insensitivity and combined targeting can restore sensitivity. (PubMed)

Palbociclib commonly induces a senescence-like G0/G1 arrest in responsive cells. Whether baseline upregulated senescence markers predict sensitivity is context dependent; senescence can be reversible or produce SASP with mixed consequences. (PubMed)

mTORC1 hyperactivation can enable escape from CDK4/6 inhibition and promote survival; conversely, sustained mTORC1 activity during arrest can promote irreversible senescence in some models. mTOR inhibitors can reverse resistance in certain preclinical/clinical contexts. (PubMed Central)

Upregulated PD-1 co-inhibitory signaling on tumor-infiltrating T cells marks an “exhausted” state driven by chronic antigen exposure and PD-L1/PD-L2 engagement. Pembrolizumab directly targets PD-1, restoring TCR signaling and effector function. Thus, tumors with higher baseline PD-1 pathway activity (e.g., PD-1⁺ exhausted CD8⁺ T cells) are more likely to benefit from PD-1 blockade.

High baseline PD-L1 expression on tumor and/or immune cells (e.g., CPS ≥10 in TNBC) reflects active PD-1/PD-L1 immune evasion. Pembrolizumab binds PD-1 on T cells, disrupting this inhibitory axis. Clinical data in TNBC (KEYNOTE-355, KEYNOTE-522) show that PD-L1-high tumors derive greater benefit from pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy than PD-L1-low tumors.

Active TCR signaling (e.g., clonal expansion and activation of tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells) underlies an inflamed, antigen-experienced TME. Transcriptomic studies in breast cancer show that T-cell–inflamed/TCR-active gene signatures, including cytotoxic and interferon-γ–related modules, correlate with response to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, including pembrolizumab in TNBC.

Upregulation of T-cell activation programs (CD28 costimulation, CD3/TCR complex, IFN-γ production, granzyme/perforin genes) marks “hot” tumors with pre-existing anti-tumor immunity. In breast cancer, high TILs and T-cell activation signatures are associated with improved outcomes and with better response to checkpoint blockade, especially in TNBC.

Interferon-γ and certain interleukins engage JAK1/2 and STAT1/STAT3 to induce antigen-presentation genes (HLA, B2M), chemokines (CXCL9/10/11), and immune-effector programs. Upregulated IFN-γ/JAK-STAT1 pathways at baseline define the “T-cell-inflamed” gene signature that predicts benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 blockade across cancers, including TNBC cohorts treated with pembrolizumab. Conversely, JAK1/2 loss-of-function is a resistance mechanism.

Higher expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., IFN-γ, CXCL9/10/11, CCL5) in the tumor and stroma promotes recruitment and retention of effector T cells and NK cells. In TNBC, chemokine-rich, immune-inflamed transcriptomic subtypes are enriched for response to pembrolizumab-based regimens, whereas immune-cold subtypes with low cytokine signaling show poor benefit.

Activation of TGF-β signaling in tumor cells and stromal fibroblasts promotes extracellular-matrix remodeling, exclusion of CD8⁺ T cells from tumor nests, differentiation of Tregs, and myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) recruitment. High TGF-β/EMT/exclusion signatures in breast and other solid tumors are associated with primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors; dual TGF-β plus PD-L1 blockade can reverse this phenotype in preclinical models.

Within effector T cells and antigen-presenting cells, NF-κB activation downstream of TCR/CD28 and pattern-recognition receptors drives production of IL-2, IFN-γ, and inflammatory chemokines that sustain antitumor immunity. Tumors with NF-κB–linked inflammatory signatures (often overlapping with IFN-γ and chemokine modules) tend to be more immune-inflamed and can respond better to PD-1 blockade, including pembrolizumab, provided that NF-κB is not dominantly tumor-intrinsic and immunosuppressive.

High VEGF signaling promotes abnormal, leaky vasculature, hypoxia, and endothelial anergy, all of which limit effector T-cell trafficking into the tumor and support immunosuppressive myeloid populations. Across multiple solid tumors, including breast cancer, elevated VEGF/hypoxia/angiogenesis signatures are associated with reduced benefit from checkpoint inhibitors, while combining anti-VEGF agents with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade can partially overcome this resistance.

HER2-amplified breast cancers show overexpression of HER2 and increased ligand-dependent HER2/HER3 and HER2/EGFR dimerization, driving strong ErbB signaling. Pertuzumab binds subdomain II of HER2 and blocks these heterodimers, especially HER2/HER3, shutting down downstream HER2-driven signaling. Tumors with high baseline HER2 activity are thus more likely to benefit from pertuzumab-containing regimens.

In HER2-positive breast cancer, HER2 overexpression leads to phosphorylation of HER2/HER3 and recruitment of PI3K, activating AKT and mTOR, a central survival/metabolic pathway. This hyperactivation is a hallmark of HER2 dependence and a key target of HER2 blockade. However, mutations in PIK3CA or PTEN loss can maintain PI3K–AKT activity even when HER2 is inhibited, contributing to primary or acquired resistance, so the relationship is “up → on-target but context-dependent sensitivity.”

Baseline HER2 overexpression can also activate RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK. Many HER2+ tumors rely on both PI3K and MAPK signaling; HER2 blockade (trastuzumab + pertuzumab) reduces ERK phosphorylation and mitogenic signaling. Tumors whose proliferation is strongly HER2→MAPK-driven tend to respond; however, MAPK-activating mutations can rewire dependence and drive resistance by shifting cells from AKT to MEK/ERK dependence independent of HER2.

HER2+ breast cancers are typically highly proliferative, with elevated cyclin D/E, CDK2/4/6, and E2F target gene expression—reflected in high Ki-67 and cell-cycle gene-set enrichment. HER2 blockade (with pertuzumab ± trastuzumab and chemotherapy) induces G1 arrest and decreased proliferation. High baseline HER2-driven proliferation is a marker of an “oncogene-addicted” state in which perturbing HER2 yields large anti-proliferative effects.

HER2+ tumors commonly exhibit reduced pro-apoptotic signaling and increased anti-apoptotic factors (via PI3K–AKT and other survival pathways). This low baseline apoptosis reflects strong dependence on HER2-mediated survival cues. When HER2 is blocked by pertuzumab (often with trastuzumab and chemo), survival signals collapse, mitochondrial and caspase pathways are activated, and apoptosis increases. Tumors whose survival is tightly linked to HER2 signaling are more likely to undergo apoptosis and respond.

ADCC itself is triggered by the antibody, but baseline features like HER2 overexpression (high antigen density), NK-cell/monocyte infiltration, and activating FcγR polymorphisms (e.g., FCGR3A V158, FCGR2A H131) enhance ADCC once pertuzumab is administered. Tumors in immune-inflamed microenvironments with such FcγR/effector features are more likely to experience potent ADCC/ADCP and better clinical benefit from HER2 antibodies.

The approved indication for pertuzumab (Perjeta) requires HER2-positive breast cancer (IHC 3+ or FISH-amplified). These tumors show a HER2-enriched transcriptional program and strong HER2-driven signaling. This baseline HER2+ subtype status is the major clinical selection criterion and strongly predicts benefit from pertuzumab-containing regimens such as CLEOPATRA (metastatic), NEOSPHERE and TRYPHAENA (neoadjuvant), and APHINITY (adjuvant).

Baseline high E2F-target expression indicates strong RB–E2F axis activity and CDK4/6 dependence. Ribociclib keeps RB1 hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F, shutting down E2F-driven transcription; tumors with strong E2F programs are therefore particularly vulnerable. (Cell)

A high G2/M hallmark signature reflects overall high proliferation (Ki-67-high luminal tumors). Although CDK4/6 acts at G1, these tumors rely on rapid G1–S cycling; CDK4/6 blockade reduces entry into S and subsequent G2/M, leading to decreased mitotic gene expression and clinical benefit. (PMC)

Hyperactivation of PI3K–AKT–mTOR (PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, pathway-high signatures) provides alternative proliferative and survival signals that dampen reliance on CDK4/6–RB1 control. This is a recurrent mechanism of (often acquired) resistance to ET + CDK4/6i; dual targeting of PI3K/mTOR and CDK4/6 can overcome resistance in models. (PMC)

Multiple studies show FGFR1 amplification and FGFR pathway activation (→ MAPK & PI3K signaling) as a mechanism of intrinsic/acquired resistance to ER-targeted therapy plus CDK4/6i (including ribociclib). FGFR activation sustains proliferation despite CDK4/6 blockade; FGFR or MAPK inhibitors can resensitize tumors. (PubMed)

Overexpression or amplification of Cyclin E1 (CCNE1) and CDK2 activity can bypass CDK4/6 dependency, maintaining RB1 phosphorylation and G1–S progression even when CDK4/6 is inhibited. High Cyclin E1 consistently associates with poor response to CDK4/6i. (PMC)

p21 is a CDK inhibitor that reinforces G1 arrest. Preclinical ER+ breast cancer models show ribociclib sensitivity proportional to p21 levels; CDK4/6i also liberate p21 from CDK4 complexes, allowing p21 to inhibit CDK2, deepening cell-cycle arrest. Very low p21 can accompany resistance. (PubMed)

In ER+ breast cancer, p16 overexpression frequently signals RB1 pathway disruption. RB1-loss / p16-high tumors are intrinsically resistant to CDK4/6 inhibitors because the core CDK4/6–RB checkpoint is already disabled. However, p16-high with fully functional RB1 is not automatically resistant—RB status is the critical determinant. (ScienceDirect)

Sacituzumab govitecan (SG) is a Trop-2–directed ADC delivering SN-38 to Trop-2–expressing tumor cells. Trop-2 is overexpressed in many epithelial tumors including TNBC and HR⁺/HER2⁻ breast cancer. High/medium Trop-2 expression facilitates antibody binding and internalization and is associated with robust clinical benefit in ASCENT and other trials, although some activity is still seen in lower expressors.

SG’s payload SN-38 is a topoisomerase I inhibitor that stabilizes the TOP1–DNA cleavage complex, causing replication-associated DNA breaks and apoptosis in dividing tumor cells. Cells lacking TOP1 or with markedly reduced TOP1 activity are resistant to camptothecins; conversely, abundant functional TOP1 provides more targets for SN-38. Thus, baseline high TOP1 activity is mechanistically compatible with SG sensitivity, though TOP1 expression/activity is not currently used clinically to select breast-cancer patients for SG.

SN-38 is predominantly inactivated in the liver by UGT1A1 glucuronidation to SN-38G. Increased UGT1A1 activity (e.g., enzyme inducers) accelerates SN-38 clearance and reduces exposure, which is expected to decrease effective systemic anticancer activity of SG; the SG label warns against concomitant strong UGT1A1 inducers for this reason. In contrast, reduced UGT1A1 activity (e.g., UGT1A1*28/*28) increases SN-38 exposure, leading mainly to higher risk of neutropenia and diarrhea. Therefore UGT1A1 is best considered a germline PK/safety factor, not a tumor-cell pathway measurable in the breast tumor transcriptome; its relationship with efficacy for SG in breast cancer remains exploratory.
