RET signaling in ER⁺ BC activates MAPK and promotes endocrine resistance; RET fusions/overexpression act as oncogenic drivers, and selpercatinib provides deep and durable responses in RET-altered tumors (including a complete response in RET-fusion BC). A high KRAS/MAPK hallmark score mainly reflects RET pathway hyperactivation rather than intrinsic resistance, so these tumors are expected to be sensitive to selpercatinib.

RET activation can converge on mTOR/p70S6K and PI3K/AKT in ER⁺ BC, contributing to endocrine resistance. In non-breast RET-driven models, AKT–mTOR pathway upregulation is a mechanism of acquired resistance to selpercatinib that can be overcome with mTOR inhibition, suggesting that PI3K/AKT/mTOR hyperactivation not fully dependent on RET limits RET-TKI efficacy. In ER⁺ BC, co-targeting PI3K/AKT/mTOR (e.g. with everolimus or PI3Ki) plus endocrine therapy is already standard in some settings, so PI3K-high/RET-high tumors may need combinatorial approaches rather than selpercatinib alone.

In ER⁺ BC models resistant to combined CDK4/6i + endocrine therapy, RET is upregulated; gene-set analysis shows enrichment of E2F targets and other proliferation programs. RET knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition (including selpercatinib in combination with CDK4/6i) reduces cell growth partly by downregulating E2F-controlled cell-cycle genes, making high E2F activity more of a RET-driven vulnerability than a resistance marker.

High G2/M pathway activity is associated with aggressive, metastatic-prone breast cancers. In CDK4/6i+ET-resistant ER⁺ models, RET overexpression sustains growth; RET knockdown enriches for downregulation of Hallmark G2M checkpoint and blocks G2–M progression. RET inhibition with selpercatinib plus CDK4/6i/fulvestrant resensitizes these models, indicating that tumors with G2/M-high, RET-driven proliferation can be sensitive to RET targeting.

RET is overexpressed in a subset of ER⁺ BC and cooperates with ER to drive tumor growth. GDNF–RET signaling induces ER target genes and contributes to endocrine resistance, yet tumors often remain ER-positive/ER-driven. Preclinical work (e.g., RET inhibition with TKIs + aromatase inhibitors) and more recent data with selpercatinib in ER⁺/RET-high, CDK4/6i+ET-resistant models support dual targeting ER and RET, so a high estrogen-response hallmark can define a context where adding selpercatinib to endocrine therapy is rational. Your original “Down” assignment is inconsistent with this.

gBRCA1/2 or broader HRD ↓ impairs high-fidelity DSB repair. Talazoparib induces PARP trapping and replication-associated damage; HR-deficient breast tumour cells cannot repair this, leading to synthetic lethality and strong clinical benefit (EMBRACA, gBRCA HER2-negative ABC). (PubMed)

In talazoparib-sensitive tumors, accumulated DNA damage and replication stress trigger mitochondrial apoptosis (caspase activation, pro-apoptotic signalling). However, “high baseline apoptosis” is not a standard predictive biomarker; what matters is an intact apoptotic machinery that can be engaged once damage accumulates. This pathway is best tagged as mechanism-of-action / on-treatment rather than as a baseline Up/Down predictor. (SpringerLink)

Overexpression of ABC transporters decreases intracellular PARP inhibitor levels. For talazoparib, recent work highlights ABCC1 and ABCG2 as key mediators of efflux and resistance; for the PARPi class as a whole, ABCB1/BCRP (ABCG2) are well-established. Thus, baseline ↑ ABC transporter signalling in breast tumors is expected to reduce talazoparib efficacy. (ScienceDirect)

Upregulated ATR–CHK1 signalling allows tumour cells to better tolerate replication stress and repair PARPi-induced lesions, contributing to acquired or de novo PARPi resistance. Multiple models show that PARPi-resistant cells exhibit ↑ ATR activity and that ATR inhibition re-sensitizes them to PARP inhibitors (including in breast/ovarian DNA-repair–deficient settings). (Nature)

In many breast cancers (TNBC, HR+), PI3K/AKT is upregulated, supporting survival and often maintaining HR competency. Preclinical work in TNBC shows that PI3K inhibition downregulates BRCA1/2, induces HR impairment and sensitizes tumours to PARP inhibition; conversely, intact/high PI3K–AKT signalling tends to sustain HR and survival, favouring relative resistance to single-agent PARPi unless the pathway is co-inhibited. So for baseline tumour state: Up → more resistant; pharmacologic Down (with PI3K/AKT inhibitors) → sensitization. (PubMed)

ER+/HER2– tumors that benefit from tamoxifen typically have active ER signaling with high estrogen-response gene expression at baseline; tamoxifen binding to ER then suppresses this program and reduces proliferation.

Functional ESR1-dependent nuclear transcription is required for tamoxifen to act as a competitive antagonist/partial agonist. ER+ tumors with intact ER/p53 circuitry are more responsive to tam; p53-mutant or ER-downregulated states show reduced benefit. (PubMed)

High E2F/G2M and proliferation signatures (Ki-67 high, luminal B biology) are associated with higher recurrence despite tamoxifen; persisting high cell-cycle activity after neoadjuvant tam marks poor endocrine response. Thus strong E2F/G2M “Up” at baseline overall aligns with relative tamoxifen resistance. (PLOS)

Tamoxifen induces growth arrest and apoptosis more effectively in ER+ cells with wild-type p53 and intact apoptotic machinery; p53-mutant cells are more resistant to 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen in vitro and correspond to worse clinical responses. (PubMed)

IFN-stimulated gene (ISG) programs and IFN-γ–like signatures can be upregulated in tamoxifen-resistant tumors and are implicated in treatment-induced cross-resistance to tamoxifen and radiotherapy; immune-“hot” luminal tumors can have complex, context-dependent behavior, but ISG-high states are more consistently linked to resistance than to improved endocrine benefit. (AACR Journals)

Hyperactivation of PI3K–AKT–mTOR via PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, or RTK signaling drives endocrine resistance by bypassing ER dependence. Clinical and preclinical data show that mTOR or PI3K/AKT inhibition (everolimus, alpelisib, capivasertib) can restore endocrine sensitivity. (PMC)

Upregulated HER2, EGFR, IGF1R or FGFR1 drive MAPK and PI3K/AKT, promoting ligand-independent ER activation and reducing tamoxifen benefit. HER2-positive or growth-factor–addicted tumors frequently require HER2-/RTK-directed therapy in addition to or instead of tamoxifen. (PubMed)

MAPK/ERK hyperactivation (e.g. via RTKs, SPRED2 loss, GPER signaling) enhances ERα transcriptional activity even in the presence of tamoxifen, sustaining proliferation. ERK inhibition can resensitize resistant models to 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen. (PubMed)

Noncanonical Hedgehog signaling is activated in tamoxifen-resistant ER+ breast cancers, partly downstream of PI3K/AKT. Pharmacologic Hh/SMO inhibition reduces growth of tamoxifen-resistant models and restores tam sensitivity. (PMC)

EMT transcription factors (e.g. PRRX1, Snail/Twist), TGF-β signaling and EMT-like gene signatures are enriched in tamoxifen-resistant ER+ cells. EMT induction can reduce ER expression and endocrine dependence; EMT reversal or EGFR/TGF-β pathway inhibition can partially resensitize to tamoxifen. (PubMed)

NF-κB activation supports survival of “tamoxifen-tolerant” ER+ cells, and NF-κB/RelA signaling is enriched in tumors after neoadjuvant tamoxifen. Pharmacologic or molecular inhibition of NF-κB restores tamoxifen sensitivity in preclinical models. (PubMed)

In tamoxifen-resistant ER+ cells, PI3K/AKT activation increases BRCA1/BARD1 expression and HR repair capacity, supporting survival under therapy and genotoxic stress; PI3K inhibitors can downregulate BARD1/BRCA1 and resensitize to tamoxifen. Robust HR activity is thus aligned with resistance rather than endocrine vulnerability. (PMC)

Loss or downregulation of Cx43-mediated gap junctional communication is observed in drug-resistant breast cancer models, including HER2+ and ER+ disease. Cx43 deficiency via c-Src/PI3K/AKT feedback promotes EMT and tamoxifen resistance; restoring Cx43 (e.g. ACT1 peptide, overexpression) improves response to tamoxifen and lapatinib. (PMC)

Tamoxifen is a prodrug; CYP2D6 converts it to active (Z)-endoxifen. Poor-metabolizer genotypes or strong CYP2D6 inhibitors lower endoxifen concentrations and are associated with reduced tamoxifen benefit in multiple cohorts, leading to genotype- or exposure-guided dosing and guideline recommendations. (PMC)

Toremifene is a SERM that competes with estradiol for ER, suppressing ER-regulated early estrogen-response genes. ER+/luminal tumors with high estrogen-response are strongly ER-dependent and regress when this program is shut down; tumors lacking ER signaling are intrinsically endocrine-insensitive.

Late estrogen-response genes mark sustained ER transcriptional output. High scores indicate addiction to ER signaling; toremifene blocks ER and reduces these signatures, leading to tumor control. Low/flat late response suggests ER-independence and weaker benefit.

ESR-mediated signaling (ligand-bound ERα/β → transcriptional programs) is the core drug target. Toremifene requires functional ER to exert antiestrogenic effects; loss of ER or switch to ER-independent pathways reduces sensitivity.

PI3K/AKT activation provides ER-independent survival and is a well-described endocrine resistance mechanism. Tumors with modest PI3K signaling remain reliant on ER; those with strong PI3K/AKT activation are less affected by ER blockade.
Toremifene suppresses mitosis and induces growth arrest; sensitive cells show marked reduction in G2/M and cell-cycle gene expression, whereas resistant clones maintain cycling despite ER blockade.

E2F targets (S-phase and DNA replication genes) are key for proliferation. Toremifene, via ER antagonism and induction of growth-inhibitory signals such as TGF-β, can repress E2F; failure to suppress E2F is a hallmark of endocrine resistance.

Toremifene inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in ER-sensitive breast cancer cells; growth inhibition reflects both mitotic block and apoptotic cell death. Lack of apoptotic induction is a common mechanism of endocrine resistance.

Toremifene (and tamoxifen) induces TGF-β1 and associated growth inhibition in breast cancer models; TGF-β1 acts as a tumor suppressor early but can become pro-metastatic later. Effective endocrine therapy seems to require a TGF-β/Smad context that favors growth arrest rather than EMT/invasion.

Trastuzumab only works when HER2 is overexpressed and functionally drives growth. High HER2 amplification/overexpression is required for benefit; persistence of HER2 signaling via truncated p95-HER2 or alternative dimer partners can blunt response. (PMC)

When PI3K/AKT is constitutively activated downstream (PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss), cells bypass HER2 dependence and show poorer response to trastuzumab; tumors with intact/less-activated PI3K/AKT are more trastuzumab-sensitive. (PMC)

HER2 overexpression drives MAPK and PI3K pathways. If MAPK activity falls when HER2 is blocked, tumors are HER2-dependent and respond. If MAPK remains high because of RAS/RAF or other lesions, trastuzumab has limited effect. (Wikipedia)

Baseline HER2+ tumors show strong proliferation. Trastuzumab’s anti-proliferative effect relies on upregulating p27Kip1 and inducing sustained G1 arrest. Tumors with intact p27 and Rb can arrest and are more sensitive; loss of p27 or hyperactive cyclin E/CDK2 uncouples cell cycle from HER2 and mediates resistance. (PubMed)

HER2+ tumors frequently upregulate survival pathways and anti-apoptotic proteins. Trastuzumab contributes to growth inhibition and apoptosis; if apoptotic pathways (e.g. p53, death receptors, caspases) remain at least partly intact, cells can undergo apoptosis after HER2 blockade. Highly anti-apoptotic phenotypes (e.g. strong STAT3/BCL-2/survivin signaling) favor resistance. (PMC)

Trastuzumab-coated HER2+ cells are killed via ADCC when Fcγ receptors on NK/effector cells function well. High-affinity FCGR2A/FCGR3A genotypes and strong in-vitro ADCC correlate with better clinical benefit; impaired FcγR signaling or immunosuppressive TME reduces trastuzumab efficacy. (PMC)

NK cells are the main effectors of trastuzumab-mediated ADCC. Robust NK activity (perforin/granzyme, cytotoxic gene signatures) supports anti-HER2 antibody efficacy, whereas low NK activity or suppressive TME limits benefit. (ScienceDirect)

HER2 overexpression upregulates VEGF and other angiogenic factors, contributing to aggressive behavior and poor prognosis; trastuzumab can reduce VEGF expression and angiogenesis, but high VEGF/angiogenic signatures often associate with worse outcomes and have motivated dual HER2 + VEGF blockade approaches. (PubMed)

Upregulation of Jagged1/Notch1 and STAT3 is a well-characterized mechanism of trastuzumab resistance. Trastuzumab itself can induce Jagged1/Notch/STAT3 activation in some contexts, leading to increased stemness, survival, and angiogenesis; blocking this axis can resensitize tumors. (AACR Journals)

IL-6–JAK–STAT3 loops feed into STAT3 activation, promoting proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. Elevated IL-6/JAK–STAT3 is frequently reported in HER2+ trastuzumab-resistant models and contributes to maintenance of resistant clones. (Frontiers)

HER2+ tumors with EMT-like, stem-cell–like features show reduced trastuzumab sensitivity. TGF-β-driven EMT and vasculogenic mimicry have been linked to acquired trastuzumab resistance; epithelial, less-EMT tumors tend to respond better. (jcancer.org)

HER2 overexpression increases the density of target antigen, enhancing ADC binding, internalization, and intra-tumoral payload delivery. Clinical benefit of T-DXd in HER2-positive and HER2-low metastatic breast cancer supports HER2 signaling as a positive predictive biomarker, provided expression is not completely lost.

If HR or other DNA-repair arms are impaired, cells are unable to repair DXd-induced DNA damage, leading to replication catastrophe and cell death. Preclinical work shows that pharmacologic inhibition of DDR components (e.g. ATR/CHK1/WEE1) synergizes with T-DXd, mirroring the behavior of other topo-I–based regimens in HR-deficient settings.

DXd-induced DNA damage activates G2/M checkpoint pathways (ATR–CHK1, WEE1, etc.). Tumors with robust checkpoint signaling can arrest the cell cycle and repair damage instead of undergoing mitotic catastrophe, promoting resistance. Inhibition of checkpoint kinases is a rational strategy to re-sensitize to T-DXd.

The trastuzumab backbone of T-DXd can still engage Fcγ receptors on immune effector cells. Higher FcγR expression/function favors antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and phagocytosis (ADCC/ADCP) of HER2-opsonized cells, which can add to the direct payload effect. Evidence is strongest for trastuzumab/T-DM1; T-DXd is assumed to behave similarly in this respect.

CD47 delivers a “don’t-eat-me” signal via SIRPα on macrophages, suppressing antibody-dependent phagocytosis. For trastuzumab-based ADCs, high CD47 expression can blunt Fc-mediated effector functions (ADCP), contributing to immune escape and functional resistance despite HER2 targeting and payload delivery.

An IFNγ-high, T-cell-inflamed microenvironment is associated with better responses to multiple antibody-based and ICI therapies. For HER2-positive and HER2-low breast cancer, immune-inflamed tumors show stronger benefit from HER2-targeted approaches and from ADC-ICI combinations (including T-DXd + PD-1/PD-L1 blockade), suggesting that a baseline IFNγ-response signature is a favorable context for T-DXd.

Upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins such as MCL1 can buffer cells against DXd-induced DNA damage and prevent mitochondrial apoptosis. RNA-based profiling of HER2-ADC–resistant models (including T-DXd) has identified MCL1 and related survival pathways as part of resistance signatures; pharmacologic MCL1/BCL2-family inhibition is being explored to restore ADC sensitivity.

PI3K/AKT hyperactivation promotes cell survival and can attenuate apoptosis in response to HER2-targeted therapies and ADC payload–induced damage. For trastuzumab and T-DM1, PI3K/AKT activation is a well-known resistance mechanism; similar principles likely apply to T-DXd, although the potent topo-I payload may partially overcome it. Thus baseline high PI3K/AKT activity is best regarded as a resistance-associated state.
High HER2/ERBB2 expression (IHC 3+, ERBB2-high mRNA) is required for T-DM1 binding and internalization; ERBB2-high tumors have markedly higher response and PFS with T-DM1.

Global ErbB/HER2 pathway activation (amplification, phosphorylation) defines “HER2-addicted” tumors where HER2-ADC targeting is effective. Loss of HER2 signaling (HER2-low) is associated with poorer T-DM1 benefit.
Tumors without strong PI3K/AKT hyperactivation rely more on HER2 signaling; intact feedback allows HER2 blockade + DM1 payload to be effective.
RAS/MAPK hyperactivation (e.g. KRAS/NRAS alterations or RTK bypass) maintains proliferation even when HER2 is blocked, contributing to HER2-therapy resistance and likely blunting T-DM1.

Contrary to the “more mitosis = more sensitive” intuition, single-cell profiling from NJMU-BC02 showed that CDK1+/high-cell-cycle cancer cells were enriched in T-DM1-resistant cases, whereas low cell-cycle activity associated with better response.
E2F Target gene signatures are part of the high-cell-cycle program; in NJMU-BC02, aggressive proliferative states correlated with resistance rather than sensitivity to T-DM1.

T-DM1 ultimately relies on DM1-induced mitotic catastrophe and apoptosis; tumors with intact apoptotic machinery (e.g. not strongly BCL2/BCL-XL dominated) are more likely to undergo cell death once mitotic block occurs.

Strong IFNγ/immune signatures and high TILs are repeatedly associated with better outcomes and response to HER2-targeted therapies (trastuzumab ± chemo). ADCC and immune priming are also relevant for T-DM1.
Efficient internalization of HER2–T-DM1 complexes is required for lysosomal trafficking and DM1 release. Reduced endocytosis or mis-trafficking is a central resistance mechanism.
Proper lysosomal degradation of T-DM1 and export of DM1 catabolites depends on lysosomal integrity and SLC46A3; loss of SLC46A3 causes innate/acquired resistance to DM1-ADCs.
DM1 is a substrate of ABCB1; overexpression of ABCB1/P-gp reduces intracellular DM1 concentration and is a well-validated mechanism of T-DM1 resistance.

CAV1 can promote T-DM1 internalization, but caveolae-mediated endocytosis has been described as a novel resistance mechanism: hypoxia-induced CAV1 phosphorylation redistributes HER2/T-DM1, reducing lysosomal delivery and cytotoxicity.

Tucatinib is a highly HER2-selective TKI that inhibits the HER2 kinase domain with minimal EGFR inhibition, suppressing HER2-driven signaling and proliferation. Tumors “addicted” to HER2 (amplified/overexpressed) derive the greatest benefit from HER2-directed regimens (e.g., tucatinib + trastuzumab + capecitabine in HER2CLIMB).

In HER2-amplified tumors, PI3K–AKT is typically upregulated downstream of HER2/HER3, contributing to oncogenic survival. Tucatinib reduces PI3K–AKT signaling by blocking HER2. However, constitutive activation of PI3K–AKT via PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, or other lesions is a well-defined mechanism of resistance to anti-HER2 therapies; such tumors may require combined HER2 + PI3K/mTOR targeting.

HER2 overexpression stimulates RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK, contributing to proliferation. Tucatinib partially suppresses this cascade by inhibiting HER2. However, reactivation of MAPK via other RTKs or RAS/RAF lesions can bypass HER2 block and is a recognized resistance mechanism to HER2-targeted agents, so the net effect of “Up” is context-dependent.

Tucatinib is HER2-selective with minimal EGFR inhibition; strong EGFR signaling (via EGFR overexpression or EGFR-driven subclones) can maintain RAS/PI3K/MAPK output despite HER2 blockade, acting as a bypass route and contributing to resistance or incomplete responses to tucatinib-based regimens.

Notch activation promotes cancer stemness, recurrence, EMT, and resistance to multiple therapies. In HER2/neu models, Notch signaling increases after HER2 down-regulation and supports recurrence and escape from HER2-targeted therapy. Up-Notch therefore marks a biology that can undermine durable tucatinib benefit, especially when tumors switch away from HER2 dependence.

Aberrant Wnt/β-catenin is frequent in TNBC and associated with stemness, EMT, and resistance to chemotherapy and targeted therapies. In breast cancer (including HER2+ contexts), Wnt activation contributes to invasive behavior, immune exclusion, and therapy resistance. Up-regulated Wnt/β-catenin thus indicates a HER2-independent, resistant phenotype, not reversed by tucatinib.

HER2+ breast-cancer cells can activate NF-κB; constitutive NF-κB activity increases invasion and anti-apoptosis. Experimental data show that constitutively active NF-κB renders HER2+ cells resistant to anti-HER2 drugs, and NF-κB upregulation is observed in lapatinib-resistant cells, with combination HER2 + NF-κB inhibition needed to resensitize them. Tucatinib alone will not correct NF-κB-driven survival.

Hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis is a recurring theme in resistance to anti-HER2 therapies. mTORC1 upregulation sustains protein synthesis and growth even when HER2 is blocked. Clinical and preclinical data support combining HER2-targeted agents with mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus) to overcome resistance—implying that strong mTORC1 activation blunts tucatinib efficacy if untreated.

In HR+/HER2+ disease, ER and HER2 form a bidirectional crosstalk network. Strong ER signaling can maintain proliferation even when HER2 is blocked, explaining why adding endocrine therapy (e.g., fulvestrant) improves outcomes in HR+ HER2-mutant settings treated with tucatinib + trastuzumab. In pure HR+/HER2– tumors, tucatinib has no direct target regardless of ER status.

Multiple datasets in early HER2+ breast cancer show that high TILs and immune-related gene signatures correlate with higher pCR rates and better event-free survival on trastuzumab-containing regimens. Tucatinib itself is not an immunotherapy, but in common combinations with trastuzumab and/or ADCs, an immune-hot environment (TCR pathway up) is a favorable prognostic context, not a validated tucatinib-specific predictive biomarker.
